children: JSW Group has set up a separate financing company for electric trucks and buses, seeking to bridge the price gap between a roughly ₹25-lakh diesel truck and an ₹85-88 lakh electric alternative, while delivering the bigger benefit over the vehicle’s life: a total cost of ownership (TCO) that could be close to 20 per cent lower than diesel and leave operators with stronger cash flows.

Banks are already coming on board. JSW Greentech CEO Sumit Mittal said electric trucks and buses are being financed at roughly 80:20, similar to diesel vehicles, while ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Canara Bank and SBI have approved JSW’s products for financing.

“Money is the last thing that is a problem,” JSW Group Chairman Sajjan Jindal said. Banks and investors are chasing opportunities in the sector, he said, adding that JSW has established a separate company to finance vehicles and gross-cost-contract operations.

The business could cross an important financial threshold well before its new plant reaches its 15,000-unit annual capacity. Asked about break-even, Jindal said he expected Greentech to be a “very profitable business”. Mittal said it would remain in a continuous investment cycle, but “the moment we touch 3,000-4,000 units,” it would reach that threshold. That is roughly 20-27 per cent of installed capacity.

Getting there will depend on attacking the electric truck’s cost disadvantage from several directions. “The disruption is not in the upfront price, but in the total cost of ownership,” Mittal said. JSW expects electric trucks to deliver 15-20 per cent lower TCO, even as it works to bring vehicle prices closer to diesel.
How battery swapping will work for electric trucks

Battery swapping is another part of that equation. JSW is preparing swapping for trucks and will begin deploying its first 100 vehicles on a captive route. It will also offer Battery-as-a-Service, wet leases and outright purchases, giving operators different ways to manage the battery cost and charging downtime.
The trucks will offer up to 500 km of range, with JSW able to vary battery size depending on the route and application.

A diesel truck travelling about 100,000 km annually consumes roughly 40,000 litres of fuel, costing around ₹40 lakh a year at ₹100 a litre, according to JSW’s calculations. Over a 10-year life, that amounts to about ₹4 crore of diesel expenditure, against which the electric truck’s higher upfront cost has to be measured.

JSW will initially concentrate on closed-loop routes between factories, mines and ports, where predictable journeys and high utilisation make charging and swapping easier to manage. About 17,000 trucks already operate across its steel, cement and ports ecosystem. Mittal estimates 40-50 per cent of current use cases could potentially be electrified relatively quickly, with others following as charging infrastructure expands.
That captive demand could also help operators secure loans: once JSW commits to using the trucks, “banks are willing to finance,” Jindal said.

“There is a lot of private-equity capital which is waiting on the sidelines,” Mittal said, adding that large global investors were looking at the sector. “I don’t think capital is going to be constrained.”
JSW will first “incubate and start this platform, get to a certain level,” Mittal said. After that, “there’ll be a lot of options” for bringing in external capital.

title: JSW sets up financing arm for electric trucks, buses
